claim: Mammalian olfactory epithelia (OE) contain hundreds of distinct olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) subtypes.
source: Mammalian olfactory epithelia (OE) contain hundreds of distinct olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) subtypes, each of which expresses a single odorant receptor (OR) and can thereby be stimulated and/or inhibited by a distinct set of odorant molecules (Imai, 2022; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Imai, 2022 and Xu et al., 2020

claim: Each OSN subtype expresses a single odorant receptor (OR).
source: Mammalian olfactory epithelia (OE) contain hundreds of distinct olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) subtypes, each of which expresses a single odorant receptor (OR) and can thereby be stimulated and/or inhibited by a distinct set of odorant molecules (Imai, 2022; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Imai, 2022 and Xu et al., 2020

claim: Each OSN subtype can be stimulated and/or inhibited by a distinct set of odorant molecules.
source: Mammalian olfactory epithelia (OE) contain hundreds of distinct olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) subtypes, each of which expresses a single odorant receptor (OR) and can thereby be stimulated and/or inhibited by a distinct set of odorant molecules (Imai, 2022; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Imai, 2022 and Xu et al., 2020

claim: The olfactory epithelium is one of a few regions of the mammalian nervous system where neurogenesis occurs throughout life.
source: The olfactory epithelium is one of a few regions of the mammalian nervous system where neurogenesis occurs throughout life (Brann and Firestein, 2014; Schwob et al., 2017; Yu and Wu, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brann and Firestein, 2014; Schwob et al., 2017; Yu and Wu, 2017

claim: In the hippocampus and olfactory bulb, persistent neurogenesis plays vital roles in learning and memory.
source: In the hippocampus and olfactory bulb, persistent neurogenesis plays vital roles in learning and memory (Lledo and Valley, 2016; Ming and Song, 2011; Opendak and Gould, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lledo and Valley, 2016; Ming and Song, 2011; Opendak and Gould, 2015

claim: Life-long neurogenesis within the mammalian OE is generally assumed to function solely to replace OSNs that are lost due to normal turnover or environmentally induced damage.
source: By contrast, life-long neurogenesis within the mammalian OE is generally assumed to function solely to replace OSNs that are lost due to normal turnover or environmentally induced damage.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing assumption in the field, representing established knowledge

claim: OSN neurogenesis is generally hypothesized to be strictly stochastic with respect to subtype.
source: This assumption is consistent with the prevailing hypothesis that OSN neurogenesis is strictly stochastic with respect to subtype since it is based on the evidently stochastic process of OR choice (McClintock, 2015; Monahan and Lomvardas, 2015; Yusuf and Monahan, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to McClintock, 2015; Monahan and Lomvardas, 2015; Yusuf and Monahan, 2024

claim: OR choice is an evidently stochastic process.
source: This assumption is consistent with the prevailing hypothesis that OSN neurogenesis is strictly stochastic with respect to subtype since it is based on the evidently stochastic process of OR choice (McClintock, 2015; Monahan and Lomvardas, 2015; Yusuf and Monahan, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to McClintock, 2015; Monahan and Lomvardas, 2015; Yusuf and Monahan, 2024

claim: The relative quantities of distinct OSN subtypes can be altered by manipulating olfactory experience in mice.
source: Several studies have observed that the relative quantities of distinct OSN subtypes can be altered by manipulating olfactory experience in mice (Cadiou et al., 2014; Cavallin et al., 2010; Coppola and Waggener, 2012; Dias and Ressler, 2014; Fischl et al., 2014; Ibarra-Soria et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2008; van der Linden et al., 2018; Morrison et al., 2015; Santoro and Dulac, 2012; Watt et al., 2004; Zhao et al., 2013; Vihani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Unilateral naris occlusion (UNO) causes both increases and decreases in the representations of different OSN subtypes on the closed side relative to the open.
source: Olfactory deprivation on one side of the OE via unilateral naris occlusion (UNO), for example, has been found to cause both increases and decreases in the representations of different OSN subtypes on the closed side relative to the open (Santoro and Dulac, 2012; Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Santoro and Dulac, 2012; Zhao et al., 2013

claim: Bidirectional changes in subtype representations have been observed following olfactory enrichment via exposure to discrete odors in mice.
source: Similar bidirectional changes in subtype representations have been observed following olfactory enrichment via exposure to discrete odors in mice (Ibarra-Soria et al., 2017; van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ibarra-Soria et al., 2017; van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020

claim: Experience-induced changes in the representations of specific OSN subtypes have generally been attributed entirely to altered OSN survival.
source: Experience-induced changes in the representations of specific OSN subtypes have generally been attributed entirely to altered OSN survival (Cadiou et al., 2014; Cavallin et al., 2010; Jones et al., 2008; van der Linden et al., 2018; Morrison et al., 2015; Santoro and Dulac, 2012; Watt et al., 2004; Zhao et al., 2013; Vihani et al., 2020; Ross and Fletcher, 2019; Zhao and Reed, 2001), which could theoretically account for both increases and decreases in subtype representations.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: UNO reduces the overall rate of OSN neurogenesis on the closed side of the OE relative to the open.
source: Unexplained observations that olfactory deprivation via UNO reduces both the overall rate of OSN neurogenesis (Farbman et al., 1988; Cummings and Brunjes, 1994; Mirich and Brunjes, 2001; van der Linden et al., 2020) and the representations of a fraction of OSN subtypes (Coppola and Waggener, 2012; Fischl et al., 2014; van der Linden et al., 2018; Santoro and Dulac, 2012; Zhao et al., 2013; van der Linden et al., 2020) motivated a recent study to test the possibility that the birthrates of these subtypes depend on olfactory stimulation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Farbman et al., 1988; Cummings and Brunjes, 1994; Mirich and Brunjes, 2001; van der Linden et al., 2020

claim: UNO reduces the representations of a fraction of OSN subtypes.
source: Unexplained observations that olfactory deprivation via UNO reduces both the overall rate of OSN neurogenesis (Farbman et al., 1988; Cummings and Brunjes, 1994; Mirich and Brunjes, 2001; van der Linden et al., 2020) and the representations of a fraction of OSN subtypes (Coppola and Waggener, 2012; Fischl et al., 2014; van der Linden et al., 2018; Santoro and Dulac, 2012; Zhao et al., 2013; van der Linden et al., 2020) motivated a recent study to test the possibility that the birthrates of these subtypes depend on olfactory stimulation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Coppola and Waggener, 2012; Fischl et al., 2014; van der Linden et al., 2018; Santoro and Dulac, 2012; Zhao et al., 2013; van der Linden et al., 2020

claim: Subtypes with reduced representations on the closed side of the OE following UNO also exhibited significantly lower birthrates on the closed side.
source: Remarkably, subtypes previously found to have reduced representations on the closed side of the OE also exhibited significantly lower birthrates on the closed side, while subtypes with elevated representations on the closed side showed no differences in birthrates between the two sides.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from van der Linden et al., 2020, as indicated by the context

claim: Subtypes with elevated representations on the closed side of the OE following UNO showed no differences in birthrates between the two sides.
source: Remarkably, subtypes previously found to have reduced representations on the closed side of the OE also exhibited significantly lower birthrates on the closed side, while subtypes with elevated representations on the closed side showed no differences in birthrates between the two sides.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from van der Linden et al., 2020, as indicated by the context

claim: Olfactory stimulation affects the representations of specific OSN subtypes via two distinct mechanisms.
source: These findings indicated that olfactory stimulation affects the representations of specific OSN subtypes via two distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings from van der Linden et al., 2020 described in the preceding text

claim: One mechanism elevates the representations of specific subtypes via selective increases in their birthrates.
source: One mechanism elevates the representations of specific subtypes via selective increases in their birthrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings from van der Linden et al., 2020 described in the preceding text

claim: A second mechanism reduces the representations of subtypes with extremely high levels of baseline activity, presumably via shortened OSN lifespans due to overstimulation.
source: By contrast, a second mechanism reduces the representations of subtypes with extremely high levels of baseline activity, presumably via shortened OSN lifespans due to overstimulation (van der Linden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on findings from van der Linden et al., 2020, with speculation about the mechanism

claim: Open-side biases in the birthrates of specific subtypes depend on whether a mouse was in the nursing or post-weaning stage at the time of birthrate assessment.
source: Consistent with this, open-side biases in the birthrates of specific subtypes have been found to depend on whether a mouse was in the nursing or post-weaning stage at the time of birthrate assessment (van der Linden et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to van der Linden et al., 2020

claim: A set of subtypes were differentially represented within the OEs of male and female mice that were housed in a sex-separated manner.
source: Support for this comes from two separate studies that identified a set of subtypes that were differentially represented within the OEs of male and female mice that were housed in a sex-separated manner until six months (van der Linden et al., 2018) or up to 43 weeks of age (Vihani et al., 2020), and that these differences were attenuated in mice that were housed sex-combined.
evidence: Supported by citations to van der Linden et al., 2018 and Vihani et al., 2020

claim: Differences in subtype representations between sex-separated males and females were attenuated in mice that were housed sex-combined.
source: Support for this comes from two separate studies that identified a set of subtypes that were differentially represented within the OEs of male and female mice that were housed in a sex-separated manner until six months (van der Linden et al., 2018) or up to 43 weeks of age (Vihani et al., 2020), and that these differences were attenuated in mice that were housed sex-combined.
evidence: Supported by citations to van der Linden et al., 2018 and Vihani et al., 2020

claim: Several subtypes that were differentially represented between sex-separated males and females were found to selectively respond to sex-specific odors.
source: Notably, several of these subtypes were found to selectively respond to sex-specific odors (van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020), indicating that the observed differences were at least partly odor-dependent.
evidence: Supported by citations to van der Linden et al., 2018 and Vihani et al., 2020

claim: Subtype Olfr235 exhibited a higher representation in mice exposed to males.
source: OSNs in the former category were exemplified by subtype Olfr235, which exhibited a higher representation in mice exposed to males (van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020) and selective responsivity to male-emitted odors (van der Linden et al., 2018), and was previously shown to respond to musk odors (McClintock et al., 2014; Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016; Shirasu et al., 2014), whose emission by mice has not been documented.
evidence: Supported by citations to van der Linden et al., 2018 and Vihani et al., 2020

claim: Subtype Olfr235 shows selective responsivity to male-emitted odors.
source: OSNs in the former category were exemplified by subtype Olfr235, which exhibited a higher representation in mice exposed to males (van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020) and selective responsivity to male-emitted odors (van der Linden et al., 2018), and was previously shown to respond to musk odors (McClintock et al., 2014; Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016; Shirasu et al., 2014), whose emission by mice has not been documented.
evidence: Supported by citation to van der Linden et al., 2018

claim: Olfr235 was previously shown to respond to musk odors.
source: OSNs in the former category were exemplified by subtype Olfr235, which exhibited a higher representation in mice exposed to males (van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020) and selective responsivity to male-emitted odors (van der Linden et al., 2018), and was previously shown to respond to musk odors (McClintock et al., 2014; Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016; Shirasu et al., 2014), whose emission by mice has not been documented.
evidence: Supported by citations to McClintock et al., 2014; Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016; Shirasu et al., 2014

claim: Olfr235 belongs to a group of subtypes that express homologous ORs and respond to different musk odorants with varying levels of sensitivity and selectivity.
source: Interestingly, Olfr235, which expresses the OR-encoding gene Or5an11, belongs to a group of subtypes that express homologous ORs and respond to different musk odorants with varying levels of sensitivity and selectivity (McClintock et al., 2014; Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to McClintock et al., 2014 and Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016

claim: Subtypes Olfr1440, Olfr1437, Olfr1431, and Olfr1434 exhibited higher transcript levels in the OEs of mice exposed to male odors compared to their unexposed counterparts (except subtype Olfr1434, whose transcript levels were too low to be accurately assessed).
source: Notably, like Olfr235, other subtypes within this group, which includes Olfr1440 (Or5an6), Olfr1437 (Or5an1b), Olfr1431 (Or5an9), and Olfr1434 (Or5an1), exhibited higher transcript levels in the OEs of mice exposed to male odors compared to their unexposed counterparts (except subtype Olfr1434, whose transcript levels were too low to be accurately assessed; van der Linden et al., 2018; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to van der Linden et al., 2018 and reference to Appendix 1—figure 1

claim: RNA-FISH analyses confirmed that the elevated transcript levels of Olfr235 and Olfr1437 observed in mice exposed to male odors reflected greater representations of these subtypes within the OSN population.
source: Accordingly, RNA-fluorescent in situ hybridization (RNA-FISH) analyses of a subset of these ORs, Olfr235 and Olfr1437, confirmed that the elevated transcript levels observed in mice exposed to male odors reflected greater representations of these subtypes within the OSN population (van der Linden et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to van der Linden et al., 2018

claim: Subtypes Olfr912 and Olfr1295 detect the male-specific non-musk odorants SBT and MTMT, respectively.
source: By contrast, subtypes Olfr912 (Or8b48) and Olfr1295 (Or4k45), which detect the male-specific non-musk odorants 2-(sec-Butyl)–4,5-dihydrothiazole (SBT) and (methylthio)methanethiol (MTMT), respectively (Vihani et al., 2020), exhibited lower representations and/or transcript levels in mice exposed to male odors (van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020; Appendix 1—figure 1), possibly reflecting reduced survival due to overstimulation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vihani et al., 2020

claim: Subtypes Olfr912 and Olfr1295 exhibited lower representations and/or transcript levels in mice exposed to male odors.
source: By contrast, subtypes Olfr912 (Or8b48) and Olfr1295 (Or4k45), which detect the male-specific non-musk odorants 2-(sec-Butyl)–4,5-dihydrothiazole (SBT) and (methylthio)methanethiol (MTMT), respectively (Vihani et al., 2020), exhibited lower representations and/or transcript levels in mice exposed to male odors (van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020; Appendix 1—figure 1), possibly reflecting reduced survival due to overstimulation.
evidence: Supported by citations to van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020 and reference to Appendix 1—figure 1

claim: Musk-responsive OSN subtypes exhibited, on average, 3.1-fold greater quantities of newborn OSNs within the open-sides of the OEs compared to the closed in UNO-treated male mice.
source: Remarkably, musk-responsive OSN subtypes exhibited, on average, 3.1-fold greater quantities of newborn OSNs within the open-sides of the OEs compared to the closed, with all subtypes except Olfr1437 showing open-side biases (Figure 1D and E-left; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D and E-left; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E

claim: Newborn OSNs of 15 randomly chosen subtypes located within approximately the same region of the OE where musk-responsive subtypes reside comprise, on average, nearly equal quantities within the open and closed sides (1.07-fold difference).
source: By contrast, newborn OSNs of 15 randomly chosen subtypes located within approximately the same region of the OE where musk-responsive subtypes reside (canonical zones 2 and 3; Tan and Xie, 2018) comprise, on average, nearly equal quantities within the open and closed sides (1.07-fold difference; Figure 1E-right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E-right

claim: Individual iOSNs and mOSNs of specific subtypes exhibit robust and singular OR expression on both the open and closed sides of OEs from UNO-treated mice.
source: As expected, individual iOSNs and mOSNs of specific subtypes exhibit robust and singular OR expression on both the open and closed sides of OEs from UNO-treated mice, while INP3 cells co-express low levels of multiple OR transcripts, as observed previously (Fletcher et al., 2017; Hanchate et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2015; Bashkirova et al., 2023; Pourmorady et al., 2024; Saraiva et al., 2015; Scholz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fletcher et al., 2017; Hanchate et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2015; Bashkirova et al., 2023; Pourmorady et al., 2024; Saraiva et al., 2015; Scholz et al., 2016 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: INP3 cells co-express low levels of multiple OR transcripts.
source: As expected, individual iOSNs and mOSNs of specific subtypes exhibit robust and singular OR expression on both the open and closed sides of OEs from UNO-treated mice, while INP3 cells co-express low levels of multiple OR transcripts, as observed previously (Fletcher et al., 2017; Hanchate et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2015; Bashkirova et al., 2023; Pourmorady et al., 2024; Saraiva et al., 2015; Scholz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fletcher et al., 2017; Hanchate et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2015; Bashkirova et al., 2023; Pourmorady et al., 2024; Saraiva et al., 2015; Scholz et al., 2016 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: EdU-labeled OSNs of subtypes Olfr235, Olfr1440, and Olfr1431 exhibited significantly greater quantities on the open side of the OE compared to the closed side in adolescent male mice (p<0.05; 2.3-fold, 1.8-fold, and 2.5-fold, respectively).
source: In agreement with findings from scRNA-seq, EdU-labeled OSNs of subtypes Olfr235, Olfr1440, and Olfr1431 exhibited significantly greater quantities on the open side of the OE compared to the closed side in adolescent male mice (p<0.05; 2.3-fold, 1.8-fold, and 2.5-fold, respectively) (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C–F

claim: Subtype Olfr1437 did not show a significant open-side bias in EdU-labeled OSNs (p>0.05; 1.01-fold).
source: By contrast, subtype Olfr1437 did not show a significant open-side bias (p>0.05; 1.01-fold; Figure 2G), nor did two non-musk-responsive subtypes, Olfr912 and Olfr1463 (Or5b109) (1.05-fold for both subtypes; Figure 2H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Non-musk-responsive subtypes Olfr912 and Olfr1463 did not show significant open-side biases in EdU-labeled OSNs (1.05-fold for both subtypes).
source: By contrast, subtype Olfr1437 did not show a significant open-side bias (p>0.05; 1.01-fold; Figure 2G), nor did two non-musk-responsive subtypes, Olfr912 and Olfr1463 (Or5b109) (1.05-fold for both subtypes; Figure 2H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: All three normalization methods (half-section, EdU+ cells, DAPI+ area) yielded open-side biases of similar magnitude for newborn Olfr235 OSNs, with no significant differences in UNO effect sizes observed between the three methods.
source: Notably, all three methods yielded open-side biases of similar magnitude, with no significant differences in UNO effect sizes (defined as the log2 [open/closed] ratio) observed between the three methods (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Sex-separated females showed no significant difference in quantities of newborn Olfr235 OSNs on the open side of the OE compared to the closed (1.1-fold).
source: Unlike sex-separated males, sex-separated females showed no significant difference in quantities of newborn Olfr235 OSNs on the open side of the OE compared to the closed (1.1-fold; Figure 3C and E-left) and, correspondingly, a significantly lower UNO effect size (p<0.05; 14-fold; Figure 3E-right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C and E-left

claim: Sex-separated females had a significantly lower UNO effect size for newborn Olfr235 OSNs compared to sex-separated males (p<0.05; 14-fold).
source: Unlike sex-separated males, sex-separated females showed no significant difference in quantities of newborn Olfr235 OSNs on the open side of the OE compared to the closed (1.1-fold; Figure 3C and E-left) and, correspondingly, a significantly lower UNO effect size (p<0.05; 14-fold; Figure 3E-right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3E-right

claim: Sex-combined females showed a significantly greater quantity of newborn Olfr235 OSNs on the open side of the OE compared to the closed (p<0.01; 2.2-fold).
source: By contrast, sex-combined females showed a significantly greater quantity of newborn Olfr235 OSNs on the open side of the OE compared to the closed (p<0.01; 2.2-fold) and, consequently, a UNO effect size significantly greater than that observed in sex-separated females (p<0.05; 11-fold), but not significantly different from sex-separated males (0.8-fold; Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E

claim: Sex-combined females had a UNO effect size for newborn Olfr235 OSNs significantly greater than that observed in sex-separated females (p<0.05; 11-fold), but not significantly different from sex-separated males (0.8-fold).
source: By contrast, sex-combined females showed a significantly greater quantity of newborn Olfr235 OSNs on the open side of the OE compared to the closed (p<0.01; 2.2-fold) and, consequently, a UNO effect size significantly greater than that observed in sex-separated females (p<0.05; 11-fold), but not significantly different from sex-separated males (0.8-fold; Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E

claim: Sex-separated males and sex-combined females exhibited significantly greater quantities of newborn Olfr235 OSNs compared to sex-separated females (p<0.01; 2.2-fold and 3.1-fold, respectively).
source: Remarkably, compared to sex-separated females, sex-separated males and sex-combined females exhibited significantly greater quantities of newborn Olfr235 OSNs (p<0.01; 2.2-fold and 3.1-fold, respectively; Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Quantities of newborn OSNs of the SBT-responsive subtype Olfr912 showed no significant differences between sex-separated females, sex-separated males, and sex-combined females.
source: By contrast, quantities of newborn OSNs of the SBT-responsive subtype Olfr912 showed no significant differences between the three experimental groups (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3H

claim: Subtypes Olfr1440 and Olfr1431 exhibited significant open-side biases in both newborn and total OSN quantities within the OEs of UNO-treated sex-separated males, sex-separated females, and sex-combined females (p<0.05), with no significant differences in UNO effect size observed between the three groups.
source: Unlike subtype Olfr235, subtypes Olfr1440 and Olfr1431 exhibited significant open-side biases in both newborn and total OSN quantities within the OEs of UNO-treated sex-separated males, sex-separated females, and sex-combined females (p<0.05), with no significant differences in UNO effect size observed between the three groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F

claim: Non-musk-responsive OSN subtypes Olfr912 and Olfr1463 exhibited no significant open-side biases in newborn OSN quantities in any experimental group.
source: As expected, the non-musk-responsive OSN subtypes Olfr912 and Olfr1463 exhibited no significant open-side biases in newborn OSN quantities in any experimental group, although Olfr912 showed significant closed-side biases in total OSNs (p<0.01; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J), consistent with the possibility that naris occlusion protects OSNs of this subtype from overstimulation (van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J

claim: Olfr912 showed significant closed-side biases in total OSNs (p<0.01).
source: As expected, the non-musk-responsive OSN subtypes Olfr912 and Olfr1463 exhibited no significant open-side biases in newborn OSN quantities in any experimental group, although Olfr912 showed significant closed-side biases in total OSNs (p<0.01; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J), consistent with the possibility that naris occlusion protects OSNs of this subtype from overstimulation (van der Linden et al., 2018; Vihani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J

claim: Newborn Olfr1431 OSNs exhibited a significantly greater (p<0.05; 2-fold) UNO effect size in the presence of adult mice compared to the absence.
source: Remarkably, newborn Olfr1431 OSNs exhibited a significantly greater (p<0.05; 2-fold) UNO effect size in the presence of adult mice compared to the absence, reflecting open-side biases of 4.8-fold and 2.5-fold, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D

claim: UNO effect sizes for newborn OSNs of subtypes Olfr235, Olfr1440, and Olfr1437, as well as the control subtype Olfr912, were not significantly affected by exposure to adults.
source: By contrast, UNO effect sizes for newborn OSNs of subtypes Olfr235, Olfr1440, and Olfr1437, as well as the control subtype Olfr912, were not significantly affected by exposure to adults (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E–I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E–I

claim: Subtype Olfr235 exhibited significant open-side biases in mice exposed to 0.1% or 1% muscone (p<0.01; 2.4 and 2.0-fold, respectively), but not those exposed to 10% (1.2-fold).
source: Subtype Olfr235, for example, which showed no significant difference in newborn OSN quantities between the open and closed sides in unexposed females, exhibited significant open-side biases in females exposed to 0.1% or 1% muscone (p<0.01; 2.4 and 2.0-fold, respectively), but not those exposed to 10% (1.2-fold; Figure 4C-middle).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C-middle

claim: Mice exposed to 0.1% or 1% muscone exhibited significantly greater UNO effect sizes for quantities of newborn Olfr235 OSNs compared to unexposed females (p<0.05; 14 and 13-fold, respectively).
source: Accordingly, mice exposed to 0.1% or 1% muscone exhibited significantly greater UNO effect sizes for quantities of newborn Olfr235 OSNs compared to unexposed females (p<0.05; 14 and 13-fold, respectively; Figure 4C-right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C-right

claim: Open-side biases in total Olfr235 OSNs were observed in mice exposed to 0.1% or 1% muscone, with the most significant effect observed at 0.1% (p<0.01).
source: Similarly, open-side biases in total Olfr235 OSNs were observed in mice exposed to 0.1% or 1% muscone, with the most significant effect observed at 0.1% (p<0.01; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Newborn Olfr1431 OSNs exhibited a significantly greater open-side bias in mice exposed to 1% muscone compared to unexposed controls (p<0.01; 1.6-fold), but no significant difference at 0.1%.
source: In the case of Olfr1431, newborn OSNs exhibited a significantly greater open-side bias in mice exposed to 1% muscone compared to unexposed controls (p<0.01; 1.6-fold), but no significant difference at 0.1%, perhaps indicating that this subtype is less sensitive to muscone than other subtypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on data from the study

claim: Neither Olfr1440 nor Olfr1431 exhibited significant open-side biases in newborn OSN quantities in mice exposed to 10% muscone.
source: Like subtype Olfr235, neither Olfr1440 nor Olfr1431 exhibited significant open-side biases in newborn OSN quantities in mice exposed to 10% muscone, potentially reflecting substantial transnasal and/or retronasal odor transfer to the closed side of the OE at this concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on data from the study

claim: Muscone exposure did not significantly affect open-side biases in newborn or total OSN quantities of the non-musk responsive subtypes Olfr912 or Olfr1463.
source: As expected, muscone exposure did not significantly affect open-side biases in newborn or total OSN quantities of the non-musk responsive subtypes Olfr912 or Olfr1463 (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: All three musk-responsive subtypes showed significantly elevated quantities of newborn OSNs in mice exposed to muscone and ambretone (p<0.05), with Olfr235 exhibiting increases of 3.2 and 3.8-fold, Olfr1440 exhibiting increases of 2.3 and 2.6-fold, and Olfr1431 exhibiting increases of 1.7 and 1.5-fold, respectively.
source: Relative to unexposed controls, all three musk-responsive subtypes showed significantly elevated quantities of newborn OSNs in mice exposed to muscone and ambretone (p<0.05), with Olfr235 exhibiting increases of 3.2 and 3.8-fold, Olfr1440 exhibiting increases of 2.3 and 2.6-fold, and Olfr1431 exhibiting increases of 1.7 and 1.5-fold, respectively (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4D–F

claim: None of the three musk-responsive subtypes exhibited significant changes in newborn OSN quantities in mice exposed to the non-musk odorants SBT or IAA.
source: By contrast, none of the three musk-responsive subtypes exhibited significant changes in newborn OSN quantities in mice exposed to the non-musk odorants SBT or IAA.
evidence: This is based on data from the study

claim: The SBT-responsive subtype Olfr912 exhibited no significant changes in quantities of newborn OSNs in mice exposed to muscone, ambretone, or SBT.
source: Likewise, the SBT-responsive subtype Olfr912 exhibited no significant changes in quantities of newborn OSNs in mice exposed to muscone, ambretone, or SBT (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C-left).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C-left

claim: Two non-musk-responsive subtypes that were previously found to undergo occlusion-dependent reductions in neurogenesis, Olfr827 and Olfr1325, showed no significant changes in quantities of newborn OSNs in mice exposed to muscone.
source: Moreover, two non-musk-responsive subtypes that were previously found to undergo occlusion-dependent reductions in neurogenesis (van der Linden et al., 2020), Olfr827 (Or9k7) and Olfr1325 (Or13ae2), showed no significant changes in quantities of newborn OSNs in mice exposed to muscone (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C-middle, right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C-middle, right and citation to van der Linden et al., 2020

claim: All three musk-responsive subtypes showed elevated quantities of newborn OSNs in adult mice exposed to muscone relative to unexposed controls, with Olfr235, Olfr1440, and Olfr1431 exhibiting 1.5-fold, 2.2-fold, and 1.9-fold increases, respectively.
source: Remarkably, despite the generally reduced OSN birthrate in adult mice compared to adolescents, all three musk-responsive subtypes showed elevated quantities of newborn OSNs in mice exposed to muscone relative to unexposed controls, with Olfr235, Olfr1440, and Olfr1431 exhibiting 1.5-fold, 2.2-fold, and 1.9-fold increases, respectively (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5C–E

claim: Observed increases in newborn OSNs of musk-responsive subtypes in adult mice exposed to muscone reached statistical significance (p<0.05) only for subtype Olfr1440.
source: Notably, observed increases reached statistical significance (p<0.05) only for subtype Olfr1440, likely due to the higher baseline birthrate of this subtype relative to Olfr235 and Olfr1431.
evidence: This is based on data from the study with speculation about the reason

claim: Exposure to muscone did not significantly increase quantities of newborn OSNs of subtype Olfr912 in adult mice.
source: As expected, exposure to muscone did not significantly increase quantities of newborn OSNs of subtype Olfr912 (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5F

claim: In sex-separated males, robust open-side biases and statistically indistinguishable UNO effect sizes were observed at 4 and 7 days post-EdU for quantities of EdU-labeled OSNs of subtypes Olfr235, Olfr1440, and Olfr1431.
source: In sex-separated males, robust open-side biases and statistically indistinguishable UNO effect sizes were observed at 4 and 7 days post-EdU for quantities of EdU-labeled OSNs of subtypes Olfr235, Olfr1440, and Olfr1431 (Figure 6C and D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6C and D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: UNO-treated and muscone-exposed females exhibited robust open-side biases in quantities of newborn Olfr235 OSNs and statistically indistinguishable UNO effect sizes at 4 and 7 days post-EdU.
source: Likewise, UNO-treated and muscone-exposed females exhibited robust open-side biases in quantities of newborn Olfr235 OSNs and statistically indistinguishable UNO effect sizes at 4 and 7 days post-EdU (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: No significant open-side biases in EdU-labeled OSN quantities or UNO effect sizes were observed at either 4 or 7 days post-EdU for subtypes Olfr912 or Olfr1463 in UNO-treated male or female mice exposed to muscone.
source: As expected, no significant open-side biases in EdU-labeled OSN quantities or UNO effect sizes were observed at either 4 or 7 days post-EdU for subtypes Olfr912 or Olfr1463 in UNO-treated male (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E) or female mice exposed to muscone (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), or for subtype Olfr235 in sex-separated females (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E, F, G

claim: Non-occluded mice exhibited statistically indistinguishable muscone-dependent increases at 4 and 7 days post-EdU for quantities of newborn OSNs of the musk-responsive subtypes Olfr235, Olfr1440, and Olfr1431.
source: Consistent with UNO-based findings, non-occluded mice exhibited statistically indistinguishable muscone-dependent increases at 4 and 7 days post-EdU for quantities of newborn OSNs of the musk-responsive subtypes Olfr235, Olfr1440, and Olfr1431 (Figure 6G-right), as well as the control subtype Olfr912 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6G-right and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H

claim: GC-MS analyses of mouse preputial gland extracts revealed the presence of molecules whose GC-MS signals are structurally consistent with known musk molecules.
source: Intriguingly, these analyses revealed the presence of molecules whose GC-MS signals are structurally consistent with known musk molecules (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2

claim: A potential match to one GC-MS signal from mouse preputial glands is cycloheptadecanol, a musk molecule that is structurally similar to those known to activate Olfr235 and Olfr1440 OSNs.
source: A potential match to one such signal is cycloheptadecanol, a musk molecule that is structurally similar to those known to activate Olfr235 and Olfr1440 OSNs (Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on GC-MS data and citation to Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016

claim: The exposure of mice to discrete odorants can selectively accelerate the birthrates of OSN subtypes that they stimulate.
source: Here, using scRNA-seq-based and histological approaches, we have found that UNO treatment of adolescent male mice reduces quantities of newborn OSNs of musk-responsive subtypes on the closed side of the OE relative to the open, consistent with the possibility that these subtypes have a capacity to undergo stimulation-dependent neurogenesis (Figures 1 and 2). Additionally, we have presented findings that the exposure of mice to male-specific odors or two different exogenous musk odorants can selectively elevate quantities of newborn OSNs of musk-responsive subtypes (Figures 3—5). Finally, we have described evidence that odor-driven increases in newborn OSN quantities are stable over time after EdU labeling, indicating that the observed changes reflect altered OSN birthrates as opposed to altered OSN lifespan or OR gene switching (Figure 6). Collectively, these findings support the hypothesis that the stimuli that regulate the birthrates of specific subtypes are discrete odors that selectively stimulate those subtypes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data presented in the study

claim: Odor-driven increases in newborn OSN quantities reflect altered OSN birthrates as opposed to altered OSN lifespan or OR gene switching.
source: Finally, we have described evidence that odor-driven increases in newborn OSN quantities are stable over time after EdU labeling, indicating that the observed changes reflect altered OSN birthrates as opposed to altered OSN lifespan or OR gene switching (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figure 6

claim: The signaling capacity for stimulation-dependent neurogenesis may be limited to only a fraction of OSN subtypes.
source: Findings from the present study and a previous one (van der Linden et al., 2020) indicate that this signaling capacity may be limited to only a fraction of OSN subtypes, since a majority of subtypes do not appear to exhibit stimulation-dependent neurogenesis (van der Linden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on findings from the current study and citation to van der Linden et al., 2020

claim: Persistent neurogenesis within the OE may serve an adaptive function in addition to the known homeostatic one.
source: These findings suggest the possibility that persistent neurogenesis within the OE serves an unknown adaptive function in addition to the known homeostatic one.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study

claim: The acceleration of the birthrates of specific OSN subtypes could selectively enhance sensitivity to odors detected by those subtypes by increasing their representations within the OE.
source: It is conceivable, for example, that the acceleration of the birthrates of specific OSN subtypes could selectively enhance sensitivity to odors detected by those subtypes by increasing their representations within the OE (van Drongelen et al., 1978; Meisami, 1989; D'Hulst et al., 2016; Apfelbach et al., 1991).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to van Drongelen et al., 1978; Meisami, 1989; D'Hulst et al., 2016; Apfelbach et al., 1991

claim: Exposure to specific odors can dramatically increase sensitivity to them in both rodents and humans.
source: This effect could have relevance to intriguing and unexplained observations in both rodents and humans that exposure to specific odors can dramatically increase sensitivity to them (Wang et al., 1993; Yee and Wysocki, 2001; Dalton et al., 2002; Voznessenskaya et al., 1995; Wang et al., 2004; Wysocki et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 1993; Yee and Wysocki, 2001; Dalton et al., 2002; Voznessenskaya et al., 1995; Wang et al., 2004; Wysocki et al., 1989

claim: OSNs produced via odor-dependent neurogenesis could conceivably enable the formation of new OB glomeruli and synaptic connections with projection neurons.
source: Alternatively, or in addition, OSNs produced via odor-dependent neurogenesis could conceivably enable the formation of new OB glomeruli and synaptic connections with projection neurons (Zou et al., 2009; Yamada et al., 2017; Dorrego-Rivas and Grubb, 2022; Qiu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Zou et al., 2009; Yamada et al., 2017; Dorrego-Rivas and Grubb, 2022; Qiu et al., 2021

claim: Musk odors are naturally emitted by numerous mammalian species.
source: Results of the present study demonstrate that the birthrates of musk-responsive subtypes can be regulated by exposure to musk odors, a group of molecules that are naturally emitted by numerous mammalian species (Asada et al., 2012; Ruzicka et al., 1926; Ward and van Dorp, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Asada et al., 2012; Ruzicka et al., 1926; Ward and van Dorp, 1981

claim: For some mammals, musk odors are known to function in attracting mates, marking territory, and deterring predators.
source: For some mammals, musk odors are known to function in attracting mates, marking territory, and deterring predators (Mookherjee and Wilson, 2012; Agosta, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mookherjee and Wilson, 2012; Agosta, 1992

claim: Exposure to musk odors has been reported to cause physiological changes in some mammals, including humans.
source: Moreover, exposure to musk odors has been reported to cause physiological changes in some mammals, including humans, suggesting that they can function as semiochemicals (Fukui et al., 2007; Kato et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fukui et al., 2007; Kato et al., 2004

claim: Musk odors have been found to be selectively attractive to male mice.
source: In mice, the physiological functions of musk odors, if any, are unknown, although they have been found to be selectively attractive to male mice (Horio et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horio et al., 2019

claim: Exogenous musk odors activate a small number of related and evolutionarily conserved mouse ORs.
source: Previous findings that exogenous musk odors activate a small number of related and evolutionarily conserved mouse ORs (McClintock et al., 2014; Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016; Shirasu et al., 2014) and that odors emitted selectively by male mice activate OSN subtypes that express a subset of these ORs (van der Linden et al., 2018) suggest the possibility that mice also emit musk-like molecules.
evidence: Supported by citations to McClintock et al., 2014; Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016; Shirasu et al., 2014

claim: Odors emitted selectively by male mice activate OSN subtypes that express a subset of musk-responsive ORs.
source: Previous findings that exogenous musk odors activate a small number of related and evolutionarily conserved mouse ORs (McClintock et al., 2014; Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016; Shirasu et al., 2014) and that odors emitted selectively by male mice activate OSN subtypes that express a subset of these ORs (van der Linden et al., 2018) suggest the possibility that mice also emit musk-like molecules.
evidence: Supported by citation to van der Linden et al., 2018

claim: Mouse odor profiles vary considerably as a function of age and sex.
source: Indeed, mouse odor profiles are known to vary considerably as a function of age and sex (Osada et al., 2008; Osada et al., 2003; Schwende et al., 1986; Stopková et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Osada et al., 2008; Osada et al., 2003; Schwende et al., 1986; Stopková et al., 2023

claim: Mouse preputial glands have a high degree of histomorphological, transcriptomic, and molecular similarities to muskrat scent glands.
source: Interestingly, mouse preputial glands have been found to have a high degree of histomorphological, transcriptomic, and molecular similarities to muskrat scent glands (Han et al., 2022), which secrete musk odors (Mookherjee and Wilson, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Han et al., 2022 and Mookherjee and Wilson, 2012

claim: A previous study noted preliminary evidence that mouse preputial gland extracts contain compounds that activate Olfr1440 OSNs.
source: Moreover, a previous study noted preliminary evidence that mouse preputial gland extracts contain compounds that activate Olfr1440 OSNs (Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sato-Akuhara et al., 2016
